I've found that making custom characters runs hand in hand with re-evaluating current characters.  Coming up with new ideas is awesome, but in the process you start to notice card interactions that you never did before, or notice the bits in current characters that don't work as well as they could.

Its not a question of Expatriette/Fixer/Bunker being "broken".  Its wondering why certain choices/cards were designed the way they were.  Its trying  to figure out their central mechanics, roles, and the "whys" and "hows" behind the wording.

Occasionally, in this process, I come up with ideas about how to enhance a specific aspect of that character or rework their deck to emphasize what I consider to be their core mechanic. This is usually done to make a character who has been relegated to the box by my friends as "weak" or as more of an anchor to be carried (Bunker) more fun to play and rewarding for the group.  In the case of Expatriette, it is because I had a string of bad games where I couldn't get any guns out until turn 3,4, or 5.

I think that's part of the problem that we, collectively, have:  the majority of our evidence is colloquial, qualitative impression; the quantitative data that's available isn't deep enough to actually provide insight into her strengths and weaknesses.

Believe it or not, for the first time I actually had one of the "no-gun" draws about two weeks back–I ran Expatriette for a solid 5 turns with nary a firearm in sight.  While I was a little astounded by this–even more so considering that in that span I pulled two Arsenal Access cards, both of which gave me Flak Jackets and a hand full of ammo–I didn't really feel that she was ineffective.  I played two RPG Launchers, taking out the Environment and keeping up with damage.  I played Speed Loading and Hairtrigger Reflexes, so that I'd be ready for when those guns came into play, and I had Flak Jackets taking big-damage hits, so I stayed at near-max health.  I did take a turn to double-draw, which disappointed me at the time, but I was pretty well set for when that first gun (an Assault Rifle) came up.

The complaints that I see–and this entirely an exaggerated perspective and summary; I don't want to put words in anyone's mouths, nor do I intend to mock in any way–boil down to two main ideas:

  1. "I don't like not being able to choose the cards I want, for a given in-game situation."

  2. "I don't like not being able to have enough cards to run all of Expatriette's options."

 

To the first complaint, I can sympathize (how many times have we all needed that one card to kill an Ongoing, only to have it at the bottom of the deck?), but the randomization of cards essentially is what makes the game unpredictable.  I compare Expatriette to Nightmist in this respect.  Call Forth and Arsenal Access are both pretty similar cards, boiled down to it–both provide random equipment.  CF pulls more, but requires discard and puts the cards in Nightmist's hand, while AA puts less cards directly into play with no discard.  Nightmist can't control the cards she gets–I can't count the times I've begged for a Amulet of the Elder Gods and all I get are Elder Rings and Tomes.  That doesn't make her underpowered–it just means that you, as the player, have to be crafty in how you play.

I find that I tend to not enjoy Heroes that have a specific "build order".  Absolute Zero and Argent Adept, for instance, often require specific plays in a specific order to be effective.  AA almost always starts off with "Song, Song, Instrument" or some variation thereon that provides that end result.  Wraith, too, to a degree, suffers from this.  I've made the argument in the equally long Mr. Fixer thread that he's often seen as underpowered because he–and Expatriette–do not have this set direction of play.  Rather, they're more free-form.  While this can potentially limit their "ceiling" of effectiveness, it doesn't make them underpowered in any sense.  I like that, as I feel freer to roll with the proverbial punches.

To the second complaint, I feel like the argument is unfounded.  I compare Expatriette to The Scholar in this respect.  The Scholar runs through cards like water when he has more than 2 or 3 Elemental Forms out, and surely has difficulty operating all of them at once, in terms of both card economy and in the fact that the Forms often run at cross purposes.  If you have Flesh to Iron out, you're not likely going to be taking a lot of damage, which means that keeping Solid to Liquid out is overkill.  Sure, it'd be nice to have enough cards to become a juggernaut of Liquid/Energy forms, but it's not realistically going to happen without significant outside contribution.  

Expatriette, in this vein, can't (and shouldn't) be able to operate everything at once.  Every 'play' segment that you spend throwing down a new Gun means an Ammo card doesn't come out, and vice versa.  Every time you use the Shotgun is an opportunity lost to use the Assault Rifle or Pride/Prejudice.  If you're cycling ammo with Speed Loading, you likely won't Unload any time soon.  That's okay.  Those opportunity costs provide the choices that make seemingly similar choices different, based on the situation.

TD:LR?  I like Expat as she is.  Same with Fixer.  I'm still going to tinker, now and again, but only to see what happens, not to "fix them" in any sense.

So, this is coming from the perspective of someone who almost always plays 4-5 person games.

I want to fix Expatriette.  I want to fix Bunker.  (Mr Fixer is awesome, though I prefer to play him when someone else is playing TL Tach.)

The reason I want to fix Expat is because playing her in a 4-5 person game can be incredibly frustrating.  Expat needs her guns.  if you don't start with one, you are pretty much frozen until you can get one. You are forced to wait until you get one. You can play speed loading and flak jackets and hair trigger reflexes, (if you have them), or (in some cases) sit there looking at a fistful of ammo, reloads, unloads, and flak Jackets.

Well, back to drawing cards. 

 

oops!  you have to get rid of equipment cards!  Will it be Wraith, who has been effective this entire time?  Maybe Haka, who has been steadily killing enemies?  Oh, I know- it should be Unity! 

 

No.  Its going to be Expatriette, since she hasn't been useful at all.

So you go back to hoping for a gun.  turn 5 rolls around and you get a shotgun.  You beg for your teammates to let you land the killing blow.

 

Unity does it instead.

Except that they're either Equipment or targets.  Relic is a "subtype", if you will.  Ra's Staff is an Equipment "supertype" with the Relic subtype, like Fanatic's Absolution or Aegis or Nightmist's Tomb/Amulet/Necklace/Ring.  A hero Relic is an Equipment card, but not all hero Equipment cards are Relics.  The Matriarch's Mask is a target with the Relic subtype.  Her Relics and Apostate's Relics are villain targets, but not all villain targets are Relics.  There are no cards that are just a Relic.  The Tomb of Anubis's Relics are one notable exception, but Environment cards are a bit strange as they aren't as categorized as Hero/Villain cards, and they can be destroyed by cards that destroy Environment cards (unlike cards with the Drug, Victim, or non-target Diversion supertype, which have no hero card that can specifically destroy those types of cards (Cedistic Dissonant is an exception to this with any non-indestructible cards)).

The difference is that though certain keywords have appeared on multiple card types, they do not change the card type itself.  Tachyon has Burst Ongoings and One-Shots, but they're never just a Burst card.  If anything, the Tomb of Anubis sneakily redefined that barrier before Miss Information came along, so I missed noticing that at first glance!  But Environment cards seem to work in a different fashion than other cards, since they've always had a history of non-target Environment cards coming into play.  Environment targets are probably the only example of two supertypes clashing together, up until Distraction targets.

Huh...I learned something today.

posts.name: Reckless
posts.cooked:
AH, yes!  My classification system is as follows:

Each card has only one supertype (except for Environment targets, as the Environment deck behaves in a different manner than the hero and villain decks), and not all cards have a subtype.  Subtypes typically interact with the mechanics in the deck itself, but they sometimes impact other decks (such as Big O and O-X's Components, Relics, or Distortions).  Typically Ongoing/Equipment/One-Shot/Target/(Environment) is enough to classify a card, and the other supertypes are notable exceptions in one deck at most.  Miss Information's Distraction cards are also a notable exception to this system.

Supertype:  Ongoing, Equipment, Target, One-Shot, Victim, Drug, (Environment), Distraction*
Subtype:  Module, Burst, Mode, Relic, Tool, Style, Gun, Spell, Rhythm, Harmony, Melody, Bounty, Component, Elemental, Trap, Distraction*, and any others that I may have missed.
Other:  Keywords on targets (Citizen, Appendage, Dinosaur, Limb, etc.).  This can range from a mechanical benefit (Thoration DR on a Gene-Bound Guard, Citizen's regaining 1 HP a turn, etc.) to pure flavor (Sheriff Pratt's "The Law" keyword).  Typically describing something as a Target is enough, but individual deck mechanics may come into play with specific keywords.  There are just a lot of these to go through, and I haven't taken the time to look them over!
???:  Environment cards.  They fit into the Hero/Villain/Environment card trinity, but they're also a "supertype" to be destroyed ("Destroy an Ongoing card" is essentially on a similar scale to "Destroy an Environment card").  They also get a little weird since they have cards that are not targets and no Ongoing/Equipment cards.  They are the only card in this classification system that can be two supertypes at once (other than 1st Ed. Visionary's Decoy Projection when it was an Ongoing Target, and Miss Information's Distraction Targets).
*An exception to the rule, like whatever the Environment Relics would be classified as.

These descriptors aren't terribly important.  They could be "Big" and "Small", or "Alpha" and "Omega".  It doesn't really matter.  It just helps me categorize the different card types.
